note: Both use the moon's spot: the Naladiyar to say the noble cannot bear one stain as the moon does, the Neelakesi to say a work, like the moon, may carry a fault and still be loved.
teaches: The same image yields opposite counsel: for a person's character a single stain is unbearable, but for a poet before an assembly an acknowledged fault is excusable.

gains.a: the poet's apology is seen to lower the standard the ethics books set for the noble
gains.b: the quatrain's rule is shown to be about moral stain, not every imperfection

note: The Kural says the fivefold sense-knowledge is fruitless without true understanding; Manimekalai tells the materialist, who trusts the senses alone, that true things are hard to know without true understanding.
teaches: The couplet's general claim becomes a debating move: the heroine uses its contrast between sense-knowledge and true understanding to show that a perception-only rule cannot reach even one's parentage.

gains.a: Manimekalai's rebuttal gains a classical Tamil statement of the same limit on the senses
gains.b: the couplet gains a concrete opponent, the materialist, whom its limit refutes

note: The couplet says all pains rest on those who caused pain; the venba says dharma is death to the wrongdoer, but the speaker, who did no wrong, calls herself one of harsh deeds and the wrongdoer's queen suffers too.
teaches: The epic agrees that harm returns to the one who did it, but shows it spreading to the innocent queen and to the victim who names her own karma, so the couplet's neat return of pain to its doer becomes a wider ruin.

gains.a: the venba's maxim gains the couplet's general rule that harm returns to its doer
gains.b: the couplet gains a case where pain does reach the doer, yet also those around him, which its own wording does not consider

note: The Sankhya speaker counts twenty-five principles with no maker; Tirumular says the Lord makes the twenty-five within the womb.
teaches: Tirumular keeps the Sankhya count and adds a maker who shapes the twenty-five for each embryo, which is the step the Sankhya account leaves out.

gains.a: the count of twenty-five gains a later life inside Saiva doctrine
gains.b: Tirumular's twenty-five gains its source in a school that counted them without a god

note: The invocation announces the debates 'beginning with the view that accepts flesh'; in the Kundalakesi debate Neelakesi charges the Buddha's path with not calling flesh-eating a fault.
teaches: The prologue names the Buddhist teaching by its tolerance of flesh, showing that the poem's first and framing charge against a rival school is ethical before it is metaphysical.

note: Both honour the feet of one who walked on the flower: மலர்மிசை ஏகினான் in the Kural, தண்டாமரைமேல் நடந்தான் in the Neelakesi.
teaches: An avowedly Jain poet uses the flower-walking epithet for his god, so the Kural's disputed epithet was current in Jain praise and not only open to other readings.

gains.a: the dream-apology is anchored in a known image of the god's feet
gains.b: the couplet's contested epithet gains a sectarian witness for one of its readings

note: Kannaki vowed to see the cruel king and ask him the reason; here she stands at his gate and sends in her charge.
teaches: The vow made beside the body is kept as a legal summons through the gatekeeper, so her grief is shown taking the form of a formal case rather than a lament.

note: Both name Pulli's Venkatam: in 61 the friend says the man would not stay even for Venkatam with its festivals; in 83 the man says her virtues followed him past Venkatam regardless of distance.
teaches: Pulli's Venkatam served akam poets as the fixed far edge of the wealth journey, and they turned it both ways: a prize too small to hold the man, and a distance too short to stop the woman's pull.

note: Kural 216 likens the wealth of the kindly to a fruit tree ripening in the middle of a town; 199 likens suppliants to birds that return to a fruiting banyan.
teaches: The Kural sees the fruiting tree from the owner's side, as wealth placed where all can reach it, while Perumpadhumanaar sees it from the birds' side, as a place to return to daily, so together they give both halves of the gift relation and make the asker's return a sign of the giver's worth.

note: The couplet calls the tears of those who cannot bear their suffering a weapon that wears away wealth; here a widow's tears and words take the king's life.
teaches: The couplet's slow wearing-away of a bad king's wealth by the people's tears becomes, in the epic, the instant death of the king at one wronged woman's tears and words.

gains.a: the venba gains a moral law behind its marvel: tears of the wronged are a force against an unjust king
gains.b: the couplet gains an extreme case, where the weapon of tears acts at once and on the king's life, not slowly on his wealth

note: The materialist makes awareness a product of the combined elements; Sivavakkiyar asks whether the dancing self is the five elements and answers with release into open space.
teaches: The tension depends on reading Sivavakkiyar's questions as rhetorical denials: the self that sees the house of release is not the elements, against the materialist for whom nothing survives their parting.

gains.a: the materialist's claim gains a Siddhar who puts the same question and answers it the other way
gains.b: Sivavakkiyar's question gains the explicit doctrine it rejects

note: The invocation's demons who lost their god's refuge are, in the story, the demons who complain to Neelakesi that the sage stopped their offerings.
teaches: The phrase 'removing refuge in the god' turns out to mean ending blood offerings, so the demons' grievance is the loss of sacrifice, the poem's first act against killing.

note: Both use the falling star and the broken royal umbrella as signs of a king's death.
teaches: The epic borrows the Sangam stock of royal death-omens but moves them into a dream before the death, turning the elegist's after-the-fact proof of grief into a warning that comes too late to be heeded.

gains.a: its dream gains a traditional sense: these are the recognised signs that a king will die, not private fears
gains.b: the poem's omens gain a narrative use, where the same signs foretell a death caused by the king's own wrong

note: The materialist calls knowledge of former births the delusion of possession or dream; in kaathai 9 Manimekalai, carried off by the deity in sleep, knew her former birth without error.
teaches: The materialist's objection names the very conditions of the heroine's own knowledge, so the epic's story stands as her unspoken answer to him.

note: Kannaki dreamed that she spoke before the king and that harm came to the king and the city with him; here she speaks before the king and he falls.
teaches: Her dream foretold both the plea and the harm beyond the king, so the king's fall here is only the first part of what the dream foretold, with the city's burning still to come.

note: The materialist's awareness arising from the elements like intoxication from mixed ingredients appears in the Neelakesi's materialist as well.
teaches: Buddhist and Jain polemic both put the liquor simile in the materialist's mouth, which suggests it was the standard Tamil way to state his theory of mind.

note: Manimekalai learns the five kinds of religion on her way to the Buddha's truth; Tirumular says those who saw the six sects did not see him.
teaches: Both texts make a survey of the sects a stage to pass through, but Manimekalai's ends in reasoned teaching and Tirumular's in clarity about a Lord the sects miss.

gains.a: the epic's tour of the schools gains a Saiva verdict on the same exercise
gains.b: Tirumular's dismissal of the sects gains a detailed record of what the sects said

note: In kaathai 26 she is told to hear each school's doctrine, see it lacks truth, and only then follow the Buddha's way, and she takes an ascetic's form to do so.
teaches: The debate chapter carries out a method laid down beforehand: hearing the schools is a prescribed stage of her training, not an open inquiry.

note: Both invocations make knowledge the mark of the god: the Kural's வாலறிவன் (one of pure knowledge), the Neelakesi's எல்லாம் உணர்ந்தான் (one who knows all).
teaches: The Kural's unnamed pure knower is open enough that a Jain poet can fill the same slot with a god defined only by omniscience and freedom from birth, with no creating role.

gains.a: the Jain invocation is seen standing in a shared Tamil form of praising the god as knower
gains.b: the couplet's sectless epithet is shown being read in a sectarian sense by a debate poem

note: The narrator's venba says the never-bent sceptre bent as the fruit of former karma; the king says only that he heeded the goldsmith and is himself the thief.
teaches: The narrator assigns the bent sceptre to karma while the king, judging himself, assigns it wholly to his own act, so the epic lets the wrongdoer refuse the excuse its narrator offers.

note: Comparison, scripture, presumption and the rest are independent means for the logician; the Buddhist teacher folds all other means into inference.
teaches: Read together, the two lists show the Buddhist reduction is aimed at a named opponent: scripture's unseen worlds lose their standing as a separate source once they must be inferred.

note: Brahma-vadin, Vaishnava and Saiva each name a different maker or keeper; Tirumular says the three gods are one in continuity and that those who divide them quarrel.
teaches: Manimekalai rejects the theistic schools for disagreeing with truth, while Tirumular faults only their division, so the same sectarian quarrel is read as error by the Buddhist and as a misunderstanding by the Saiva.

gains.a: the epic's row of competing creators gains an insider's verdict that they need not compete
gains.b: Tirumular's 'those who divide quarrel' gains a staged instance of the quarrel he condemns

note: The couplet makes inquiry (தேர்ந்துசெய்) part of what justice is; Kannaki's first words to the king name him as the one who did not inquire.
teaches: The couplet treats inquiry as within the ruler's power, while the epic shows a ruler failing it in an hour the narrator calls karma's ripening, and still holds him answerable for it.

gains.a: Kannaki's charge gains a definition: what the king failed is the first step of justice itself
gains.b: the couplet gains a case that tests it: a king fails to inquire under the press of former deeds and is still judged by the couplet's standard

note: The Sankhya speaker has space, wind, fire, water and earth unfold from intellect; Tirumular gives the same chain from மான் (mahat), in his chapter on creation.
teaches: The same sequence of elements serves the Sankhya as nature unfolding by itself and Tirumular as part of the Lord's creating, so the cosmology was shared while its cause was disputed.

gains.a: the Sankhya account gains a Tamil Saiva reuse of its sequence
gains.b: Tirumular's uncertain verse gains a fuller statement of the chain it compresses

note: The Ajivika holds the elemental atoms to be without beginning; Sivavakkiyar says the elements and senses, and even the soul, are not beginningless, and only the truth mingled with them is.
teaches: The question of what is beginningless divides the two: for the Ajivika matter itself is eternal, for the Siddhar matter and soul are both made, and only the one truth is without beginning.

gains.a: the Ajivika claim gains a direct contrary from a later Tamil voice using the same word
gains.b: Sivavakkiyar's denial gains a named opponent who held the elements beginningless

note: Here the materialist explains away dream and possession as the mind changed; the Neelakesi's Jain asks him how his elements account for dreams, mantras and omens.
teaches: The two epics use dream against the materialist in opposite directions: Manimekalai's opponent uses it to dismiss rebirth, Neelakesi uses it as evidence his elements cannot explain.

note: The Ajivika says everything a life meets is fixed at conception by prior fate; the Kural says those who strive without flagging see fate's back.
teaches: Against the Ajivika's fixed course, the couplet's claim that effort can rout fate stands out as a deliberate limit on oozh, which the Kural elsewhere (380) calls the strongest power.

gains.a: the epic's rival doctrine of total fate gains the Tamil ethical tradition's answer
gains.b: the couplet gains a full statement of the fatalism it resists

note: The logician pairs the Buddhists with சினன் and with two means of knowledge; kaathai 29 has ஆதி சினேந்திரன் teaching exactly two.
teaches: The later kaathai confirms that சினன் in the list of schools names the Buddha, so the rival's account of Buddhism here is accurate on the count of means.

note: The Saiva debater defines God as the eight forms; Pattinathar reads the eight forms and Siva's other emblems as teachings, and mocks those who whirl in word and meaning.
teaches: Set beside the debate hall, Pattinathar's verse shows the Saiva poets turning the same eight-form creed from a debating thesis into a teaching the arguers fail to grasp.

gains.a: the Saiva's bare list gains a Saiva reading of what each form is meant to teach
gains.b: Pattinathar's scorn for word-proud disputants gains a scene of such disputants at work

note: The queen's dream of the falling umbrella and sceptre is fulfilled in the king's lowered umbrella and slack sceptre at the verdict.
teaches: The omen comes first in the queen's private dream and is fulfilled the same hour in public, so the fall of justice is shown as already decided before Kannaki speaks.

note: The patikam's first moral, that dharma becomes death to those who err in kingship, is restated here as a common saying proved true.
teaches: The moral announced at the outset as the poem's thesis is here called a saying of the assemblies now proved, so the book frames its plot as the demonstration of a received maxim.

note: Kural 745 praises a fort that is hard to take, holds stored food and is easy for those inside to hold; 44 tells a besieged king that sitting secure behind shut gates and a long wall is shameful while his elephants starve and his people cry for milk and water. On the reading that both judge the king who holds out in a fort, they disagree.
teaches: The Kural values the fort as a means of holding out, while Kovur Kizhar sees the same holding out from inside, through starving beasts and infants, and calls it neither aram nor maram, so the pair shows the fort's strength and its moral cost as two views of one siege.

note: Kannaki's 'he who relieved the distress of the bird' repeats the Purananuru's praise formula for the Chola's ancestor (புள்ளுறு புன்கண் தீர்த்த).
teaches: The epic takes a genealogical compliment that a Sangam poet paid a Chola king and turns it into a legal precedent that a Chola woman holds against a Pandya, showing the ancestor-legend working as a standard of justice across kingdoms.

gains.a: Kannaki's precedent gains the weight of an established praise-formula of the Chola line
gains.b: the formula gains a use beyond flattery: it becomes the measure by which another king is judged

note: The logician's perception grasps name, class, quality and action and sits among ten means; Aravanar's Buddhist logic keeps two means and takes name, class, quality and action out of perception.
teaches: The epic stages the theory of knowledge as a reply across two kaathais: what the Vedic logician packs into seeing, the Buddhist teacher moves into inference, so the dispute is over where conceptual labels enter knowledge.

note: The couplet says a ruler who does not examine and do justice perishes by himself (தானே கெடும்); the Pandya, who did not examine, pronounces his own death.
teaches: The epic makes the couplet's 'perishes by himself' literal: no enemy or court condemns the king, he passes the sentence on himself the moment his error is shown, and he was easily approached, so only the failure to examine undoes him.

gains.a: the king's self-sentence gains a rule behind it: ruin comes from within to the king who does not examine
gains.b: the couplet gains a scene that separates its two conditions, an accessible king who still fails to examine, and shows the ruin as self-inflicted in act as well as in result

note: The venba's 'queen of the king' and the speaker 'of harsh deeds' recur at the opening of the next kaathai, where Kannaki addresses the queen and calls herself கொடுவினை யாட்டியேன்.
teaches: The next kaathai's opening supports reading this venba as Kannaki's words to the queen, and shows the threat 'see what I will do' carried into the vow against the city.

note: Both end with the two deeds turned back; the Jain does it by blocking new deeds and exhausting old ones, Tirumular by keeping the Lord's feet in mind.
teaches: The pair shows Jain and Saiva agreeing that release needs both good and bad deeds stopped, and parting over whether the stopping is one's own labour or follows from holding the Lord.

gains.a: the Jain account gains a Saiva parallel that isolates what is distinctive in its godless method
gains.b: Tirumular's line on the two deeds gains a rival technique for the same end

note: The invocation's 'unable to disturb his penance' is told at length when her terrors fail and she gives up, fearing his penance will burn her.
teaches: The story makes the sage's penance an active power that the demoness fears, which the prologue's bare statement of her failure does not convey.

note: The Kural says a fault in the well-born shows like the moon's spot; the Neelakesi says the moon's spot does not stop the world loving it.
teaches: Read together, the moon's spot is both what makes a high fault visible and what proves the loved and high are never spotless, so visibility is not the same as rejection.

gains.a: the apology answers the worry the couplet raises, that a fault in a high place is seen by all
gains.b: the couplet's warning is softened by a case where the visible spot is forgiven

note: The invocation says she took the great one's dharma and her dark heart turned; at the end of the sermon she says she has taken the clear knowledge and asks for atonement for the wrong she did.
teaches: The prologue's single word of conversion becomes, in the story, a confession and a request for expiation, so the turn is shown as moral repair and not only a change of belief.

note: Both describe the making of a hero-stone: 264's name carved, red flower garland bound with maral fibre and peacock feather; Akananuru 269's names washed, turmeric, and a karanthai garland tied with fibre on the stone by the road.
teaches: The akam poet borrows the puram rite almost item by item to fill the heroine's fear of the road, which shows that the hero-stone was a fixed, widely known ritual whose details an akam audience would recognise as danger without being told.

note: The narrator says the king did not inquire because it was the hour of karma's fruit (தேரான் ஆகி); Kannaki calls him the king who did not inquire (தேரா மன்னா).
teaches: The same failure to inquire is excused by karma in the narrator's voice and charged as guilt in Kannaki's, and she herself also names karma, so the epic holds both causes together rather than choosing one.

note: Having heard the schools in an assumed form, she later tells Aravanar that the five kinds of religion are not right and she has not kept them in mind.
teaches: The closing line's 'she learned the five kinds of religion' is completed by her verdict in kaathai 29, which turns the survey into a rejection.

note: The logician files 'these are your parents', taken on another's word, as a false semblance of knowledge; Manimekalai offers knowing one's parents as an inference no one can refuse.
teaches: The chapter's opening list and its closing argument use the same example in opposite ways, so the heroine's rebuttal is also a correction of the logician's classification.

claims.gist: those who want dharma should judge a teaching by its worth, not scorn it for its humble source
the lord is the one whom the Indras worship
the categories are dharma, adharma, time, space, soul, atoms, merit, demerit, bondage and release
every thing is both lasting and passing, and in each moment originates, persists and is destroyed
there are six categories: substance, quality, action, generality, particularity and inherence
substance bears quality and action and is ninefold: earth, water, fire, wind, space, direction, time, self and mind
earth has five qualities and the other elements fewer
inference knows the thing to be inferred through a mark
inference is of three kinds: general, from effect, and from cause
a valid reason, tied to one of the three times and free of fault, knows the unseen through the seen
a single atom is seen only by those with divine sight
beings pass in order through six births by colour and reach release in the last, white birth
the god is the knower without limit, present in all things at all times
there are five categories: the soul and four kinds of atom
atoms combine into mountains, trees and bodies and part again, while the soul is what knows
awareness arises from the elements combined, as intoxication from mixed ingredients
awareness perishes when the elements separate, like the fading sound of a drum
perception alone is a means of knowledge; inference fails
there is only this life; a next world where deeds bear fruit is false
the whole world is an egg laid by one god
Narayana is the protector
the Veda with its six limbs arises from no cause and has neither beginning nor end, and it is the path
the words of these speakers agree with no way of truth or accepted usage
taking the great one's dharma can turn even a demon's evil heart toward holiness
dharma itself becomes death to those who do wrong
one knows one's own father and mother only by inference
without true understanding the true nature of things is hard to know
atoms have no beginning, are never destroyed or newly born, and never change their kind
a compound of atoms is named for the element that predominates in it
to kill a thief is not cruel rule but the king's due justice
a king who punishes on a false word is himself the thief
a king whose guarding of the people has failed should not live
only the omniscient one, free of birth and its companions, whose teaching ends the suffering of souls, is to be praised as god
gain, loss, pleasure, pain, birth and death are all fixed at the moment of conception
pleasure and pain are themselves atoms
the fate laid down before brings about what comes after
the person is pure awareness, not of the three qualities, one, pervading and eternal
there are twenty-five principles, ending in the soul
nothing, not even the moon, is free of flaw, so a work may be accepted with its faults acknowledged
there are eight false semblances of valid knowledge
to hold on others' word that these are one's mother and father is memory, a false semblance of knowledge
six means of knowledge, perception to absence, are those current now among the six schools
a just king relieves the suffering even of a bird or a cow, though it cost his own son's life
a former deed drives a man to the place where it ripens
a king who punishes without inquiry fails in justice
comparison is a separate means of knowledge
scripture, the knower's book, gives valid knowledge of unseen worlds
presumption, tradition, absence and the rest are each a means of knowledge in their own right
God is the one who is the eight forms: sun, moon, the sacrificer and the five elements
God binds the soul to the body, creates the world in play and removes sorrow
God has nothing other than himself
some have come to know a birth before this one
knowledge of a former birth comes from possession by a god or from dreams, and is mere doubt
primal nature, made of the three qualities and without mind, is the ground from which all things appear
intellect, the elements, mind, the sense of self, the senses and the organs of action unfold from primal nature in order
the world returns the way it came into dissolution, while primal nature remains one, pervading and eternal
dharma pervades all and makes things move; adharma makes them stay
the soul joins a body and through it enjoys the senses
release is to block the inflow of both good and bad deeds and exhaust past deeds by experiencing their fruit
the truth of things must be grasped through the means of valid knowledge
valid perception is of five kinds, one for each sense
sound perception grasps a thing's place, name, class, quality and action
